name: Hydrogen

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: hydro, water, and genes, forming, because burning it makes water

summary: The lightest element and the simplest atom, one proton and one electron, and by a wide margin the most abundant substance in the universe.
uses: Ammonia for fertiliser, the refining of petroleum, the hardening of fats, and the fuel cell that turns it back into water.
sources: Bound into water, into every hydrocarbon, and into every living thing; almost none of it exists on Earth as a free gas.

name: Helium

discovery.discoveredBy: William Ramsay, Pierre Janssen, Norman Lockyer
discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: helios, the sun, where it was detected before it was found on Earth

summary: A colourless, odourless gas that will not burn, will not react, and will not freeze at any temperature a laboratory has reached.
uses: Cooling superconducting magnets in MRI scanners, lifting balloons, and shielding a weld from the air around it.
sources: Extracted from a few natural gas fields where it has accumulated from the radioactive decay of heavy elements.

name: Lithium

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: lithos, stone, because it was first found in a mineral rather than in a plant

summary: The lightest metal, soft enough to cut with a knife and light enough to float on water, which it then reacts with.
uses: Rechargeable batteries, heat-resistant glass and ceramics, and a carbonate that steadies mood.
sources: Brine beneath salt flats and a handful of hard minerals such as spodumene.

name: Beryllium

discovery.discoveredBy: Louis Nicolas Vauquelin, Antoine Bussy, Friedrich Wöhler
discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: beryllos, the mineral beryl, which also gives emerald and aquamarine

summary: A light, stiff, steel-grey metal that is transparent to X-rays and poisonous as dust.
uses: Windows for X-ray tubes, aerospace alloys, and the springs and mirrors of instruments where stiffness matters more than cost.
sources: The minerals beryl and bertrandite, in amounts small enough that the metal stays expensive.

name: Boron

discovery.nameOrigin: From borax, the mineral it was first isolated from

summary: A metalloid that forms some of the hardest known materials and some of the softest, depending on how its atoms are arranged.
uses: Borosilicate glass that survives a temperature change, detergents, and the boron rods that absorb neutrons in a reactor.
sources: Evaporated lake beds, chiefly in Turkey and California, where it is mined as borax.

name: Carbon

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: carbo, charcoal

summary: The element that forms more compounds than all the others together, and appears as graphite, diamond, and the framework of every living thing.
uses: Steel, and therefore almost everything made of steel; graphite electrodes; and diamond, which is carbon arranged to be the hardest natural substance.
sources: Coal, petroleum, limestone, the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, and every organism alive or fossilised.

name: Nitrogen

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: nitron and genes, soda forming, from its presence in saltpetre

summary: A colourless, nearly inert gas that makes up four fifths of the air, and the element every protein and every strand of DNA is built around.
uses: Fertiliser through the Haber process, refrigeration as liquid nitrogen, and an inert atmosphere for food packaging and welding.
sources: The air, which is 78 per cent nitrogen by volume; on Earth it is otherwise locked into minerals and living tissue.

name: Oxygen

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: oxys and genes, acid forming, from the mistaken belief that it was in every acid

summary: The most abundant element in the Earth's crust and the one that makes combustion and breathing possible.
uses: Steelmaking, medical breathing support, rocket oxidiser, and the treatment of wastewater.
sources: The air, one fifth by volume; water; and the silicate rocks that make up most of the planet's mass.

name: Fluorine

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: fluere, to flow, from a mineral used to make molten metal flow

summary: The most reactive of all the elements, a pale yellow gas that attacks glass and will not be tamed by anything else for long.
uses: Uranium enrichment, fluoropolymers such as the coating on a frying pan, and the fluoride that hardens tooth enamel.
sources: Fluorite and cryolite, and as a trace in apatite; never as the free element, which would react with whatever it touched.

name: Neon

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: neos, new

summary: An inert gas that glows a deep red-orange when a current is passed through it, which is the only reason most people have heard of it.
uses: Discharge lighting and signs, and a cryogenic refrigerant.
sources: The air, at eighteen parts per million, separated out by cooling air until it liquefies.

name: Sodium

discovery.nameOrigin: English: soda, and Latin natrium, from the salt it was first extracted from

summary: A soft silvery metal that reacts violently with water and has to be stored under oil, and one half of ordinary table salt.
uses: Sodium vapour street lamps, the coolant in some nuclear reactors, and, as a compound, soap, glass and salt itself.
sources: Rock salt, sea water, and the mineral feldspar that makes up much of the Earth's crust.

name: Magnesium

discovery.nameOrigin: From Magnesia, a district of Greece where its mineral was found

summary: A light structural metal that burns with a blinding white flame, and the atom at the centre of every chlorophyll molecule.
uses: Lightweight alloys for cars and aircraft, fireworks, and a compound that calms an unsettled stomach.
sources: Sea water, dolomite, and the mineral carnallite; it is the eighth most abundant element in the crust.

name: Aluminium

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: alumen, alum, the salt it was first isolated from

summary: The most abundant metal in the Earth's crust, light and corrosion-resistant, and impossible to extract cheaply until the 1880s.
uses: Drinks cans, foil, window frames, aircraft, and the electrical cables of overhead power lines.
sources: Bauxite ore, which is refined into alumina and then broken down by electrolysis.

name: Silicon

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: silex, flint, its most familiar mineral form

summary: A metalloid that makes up most of the rock and sand of the planet, and the material every computer chip is carved from.
uses: Semiconductor devices, glass, concrete, and the silicone that seals a bathroom.
sources: Sand and quartz, and the silicate minerals that form most of the Earth's mantle and crust.

name: Phosphorus

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: phosphoros, light bearer, because white phosphorus glows in the dark

summary: A non-metal that will burst into flame in air, and the element that carries energy around every living cell.
uses: Fertiliser, detergents, and the strike plate of a matchbox.
sources: Phosphate rock, and the bones and teeth of every vertebrate.

name: Sulphur

discovery.nameOrigin: Sanskrit: sulvere, and Latin sulphurium

summary: A yellow non-metal that burns with a blue flame and a choking smell, known since antiquity as brimstone.
uses: Sulphuric acid, the most produced industrial chemical; vulcanising rubber; and fungicides.
sources: Recovered from natural gas and petroleum, and found pure around volcanoes and hot springs.

name: Chlorine

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: chloros, pale green, the colour of the gas

summary: A green-yellow gas that will bleach and disinfect and, in a high enough concentration, kill; the other half of table salt.
uses: Disinfecting drinking water and swimming pools, making plastics, and bleaching paper.
sources: Sea water and rock salt, from which it is released by electrolysis.

name: Argon

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: argos, idle, because it takes part in nothing

summary: An inert gas that is the third most abundant in the air, and the one that was discovered by noticing a leftover fraction that would not react.
uses: A shielding gas for welding, the fill in a double-glazed window, and the inert atmosphere inside a filament lamp.
sources: The air, at just under one per cent, separated by fractional distillation of liquid air.

name: Potassium

discovery.nameOrigin: English: potash, and Latin kalium, from the ash it was first extracted from

summary: A soft metal that ignites on contact with water, and the ion whose movement along a nerve carries every thought you have.
uses: Fertiliser, and as a compound, glass, soap and a salt substitute.
sources: Sylvite and carnallite deposits, and every sea and every soil.

name: Calcium

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: calx, lime, the material it was isolated from

summary: A reactive metal that is the fifth most abundant element in the crust, and the one your bones and teeth are mostly built from.
uses: Cement and mortar, steelmaking, and dietary supplements.
sources: Limestone, chalk, gypsum, and the shells and skeletons of marine life.

name: Scandium

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: Scandia, Scandinavia, where its ore was found

summary: A light, rare, silvery metal whose existence was predicted before it was found, the first element to be discovered that way.
uses: Aluminium alloys light enough for bicycle frames and aerospace parts, and very bright lamps.
sources: Rare minerals such as thortveitite, and as a by-product of refining uranium and tungsten.

name: Titanium

discovery.nameOrigin: The Titans of Greek myth

summary: A strong, light, corrosion-proof metal with an excellent reputation and a price to match, named for beings of enormous strength.
uses: Aircraft, replacement joints, and the frame of a racing bicycle; and, as the oxide, a white pigment.
sources: The minerals rutile and ilmenite, which are common in beach sand.

name: Vanadium

discovery.nameOrigin: Vanadis, a name of the Norse goddess Freyja

summary: A hard silver-grey metal whose compounds come in an unusually wide range of bright colours.
uses: Strengthening steel for tools and springs, and a catalyst for making sulphuric acid.
sources: Vanadinite and patronite, and as a trace in crude oil.

name: Chromium

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: chroma, colour, from the colours of its compounds

summary: A hard, lustrous metal that takes a mirror polish and refuses to tarnish, and the reason stainless steel is stainless.
uses: Chrome plating, stainless steel, leather tanning, and pigments in paints and glass.
sources: Chromite ore; almost all of it goes into alloys.

name: Manganese

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: magnes, magnet, from the magnetic ore it was found in

summary: A brittle grey metal that is essential to steelmaking and, in trace amounts, essential to life.
uses: Deoxidising and desulphurising steel, dry-cell batteries, and the violet colour in glass.
sources: Pyrolusite and other oxide ores, and nodules on the deep ocean floor.

name: Iron

discovery.nameOrigin: Anglo-Saxon: iren; the symbol is from Latin ferrum

summary: The most-used metal on Earth, the main ingredient of the planet's core, and the atom that carries oxygen in your blood.
uses: Steel, which is to say buildings, bridges, ships, vehicles, tools and cutlery.
sources: Haematite and magnetite ores, and, in the core, most of the Earth's mass.

name: Cobalt

discovery.nameOrigin: German: kobold, goblin, for the ore that troubled Saxon miners

summary: A hard, magnetic metal that keeps its strength when hot, which is what makes it useful in an engine.
uses: Superalloys for jet turbines, the cobalt-blue pigments in glass and ceramics, and the cathode of a lithium-ion battery.
sources: Cobaltite and skutterudite, mostly extracted as a by-product of copper and nickel.

name: Nickel

discovery.nameOrigin: German: kupfernickel, Old Nick's copper, for an ore that promised copper and gave none

summary: A hard, silvery metal that resists corrosion, is magnetic, and is the element at the heart of the Earth's core alongside iron.
uses: Stainless steel, rechargeable batteries, coins, and electroplating.
sources: Laterite and sulphide ores, and, in an unusually pure form, in iron meteorites.

name: Copper

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: cuprum, from the island of Cyprus

summary: A reddish metal that conducts electricity better than anything except silver, and the first metal people learned to work.
uses: Electrical wiring, plumbing, roofing, and alloys such as brass and bronze.
sources: Chalcopyrite and malachite ores, and occasionally as native metal.

name: Zinc

discovery.nameOrigin: German: zink, of uncertain origin

summary: A bluish-white metal that is a poor conductor and a good protector, since it corrodes in place of the steel beneath it.
uses: Galvanising steel, brass, die-castings, and sunscreen as the oxide.
sources: Sphalerite, and as a trace in almost every ore of lead and copper.

name: Gallium

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: Gallia, France

summary: A soft silvery metal that melts in the palm of a hand and then refuses to boil until well past a thousand degrees.
uses: Light-emitting diodes, high-speed and high-frequency electronics, and solar cells.
sources: Never mined for itself; recovered as a trace from bauxite and zinc ore.

name: Germanium

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: Germania, Germany

summary: A metalloid whose prediction preceded its discovery, and the material the first transistor was made from before silicon took over.
uses: Fibre-optic cables, infrared optics, and polymerisation catalysts.
sources: By-product of zinc refining, and in a handful of rare minerals.

name: Arsenic

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: arsenikon, yellow orpiment, the pigment it was found in

summary: A metalloid notorious as a poison and useful as a semiconductor, with a smell of garlic when it is heated.
uses: Gallium arsenide in high-frequency electronics, wood preservatives, and alloy hardening.
sources: Arsenopyrite and realgar, and as a contaminant in copper and lead ores.

name: Selenium

discovery.discoveredBy: Johan Gottlieb Gahn, Jöns Jacob Berzelius
discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: selene, the moon

summary: A non-metal whose electrical resistance falls when light falls on it, which is the property a photocopier was built on.
uses: Glassmaking to remove the green tint of iron, photocopier drums, and a trace nutrient.
sources: By-product of copper refining, and in the soils of a few regions in quantities that are toxic rather than nourishing.

name: Bromine

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: bromos, stench, for its smell

summary: The only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature, a deep red-brown liquid that gives off an irritating vapour.
uses: Flame retardants, water treatment, and photographic film as silver bromide.
sources: Sea water and brine wells, extracted by displacement with chlorine.

name: Krypton

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: kryptos, hidden

summary: An inert gas discovered by looking for what was left over, and the one the length of a metre was once defined by.
uses: High-performance lighting, photographic flash, and insulating gas in some windows.
sources: The air, at one part per million, separated by cooling air until it liquefies.

name: Rubidium

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: rubidus, deepest red, the colour of the lines in its spectrum

summary: A soft silver-white metal that melts just above room temperature and catches fire in air.
uses: Atomic clocks, and research rather than industry.
sources: A minor component of the minerals lepidolite and carnallite.

name: Strontium

discovery.nameOrigin: Strontian, a village in Scotland

summary: A soft, reactive metal whose salts burn crimson, which is why it is in every red firework.
uses: Red colour in fireworks and flares, and ferrite magnets.
sources: The minerals celestine and strontianite.

name: Yttrium

discovery.nameOrigin: Ytterby, a village in Sweden, which gave its name to four elements

summary: A soft silvery metal used in small amounts in a wide range of materials that would otherwise not work.
uses: Phosphors in older televisions, the stabiliser in cubic zirconia, and superconductors.
sources: Monazite and bastnasite, alongside the rare earths it is always found with.

name: Zirconium

discovery.discoveredBy: Anton Eduard van Arkel, Jöns Jacob Berzelius, Jan Hendrik de Boer, Martin Heinrich Klaproth
discovery.nameOrigin: Persian: zargun, gold-like, from the mineral zircon

summary: A corrosion-resistant metal that lets neutrons pass through it, which is precisely what a reactor needs of its cladding.
uses: Nuclear fuel rod cladding, corrosion-proof chemical piping, and cubic zirconia as a gemstone.
sources: Zircon sand, a common by-product of mining heavy mineral sands.

name: Niobium

discovery.nameOrigin: Niobe, daughter of Tantalus in Greek myth, because it is found with tantalum

summary: A soft grey metal that becomes superconducting at unusually high temperatures and is found, invariably, alongside tantalum.
uses: Superconducting magnets for MRI scanners and particle accelerators, and microalloyed steels for pipelines.
sources: The mineral columbite, and as a by-product of tin smelting.

name: Molybdenum

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: molybdos, lead, because its ore was mistaken for a lead ore

summary: A hard silvery metal with one of the highest melting points of any commercial metal.
uses: High-strength steel, furnace parts that must hold their shape when glowing, and a catalyst for refining petroleum.
sources: Molybdenite, and as a by-product of copper mining.

name: Technetium

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: technetos, artificial, because it was the first element made rather than found

summary: The lightest element with no stable isotope, so every atom of it on Earth has been made by someone.
uses: A short-lived isotope that images bones, hearts and kidneys in nuclear medicine.
sources: Produced in reactors and extracted from the fission products of uranium.

name: Ruthenium

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: Ruthenia, Russia

summary: A hard, brittle platinum-group metal that is one of the rarest on Earth and unusually good at hardening other metals.
uses: Electrical contacts, wear-resistant plating, and catalysts.
sources: Platinum ores, and as a by-product of nickel refining.

name: Rhodium

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: rhodon, rose, from the colour of one of its salts

summary: A silvery-white metal, rarer than gold and far more expensive, that keeps its shine and speeds up reactions.
uses: Catalytic converters, the reflective coating on laboratory mirrors, and electrical contacts.
sources: Platinum ores, chiefly in South Africa.

name: Palladium

discovery.nameOrigin: The asteroid Pallas

summary: A soft platinum-group metal that soaks up hydrogen like a sponge, taking in hundreds of times its own volume.
uses: Catalytic converters, electronics, dentistry, and the purification of hydrogen.
sources: Nickel and platinum ores, chiefly in Russia and South Africa.

name: Silver

discovery.nameOrigin: Anglo-Saxon: seolfor; the symbol is from Latin argentum

summary: The best electrical and thermal conductor of any metal, and the one whose antimicrobial property people noticed long before they understood it.
uses: Electrical contacts, brazing alloys, photography, solar panels and jewellery.
sources: Argentite and horn silver, and alongside lead, zinc and copper ores.

name: Cadmium

discovery.discoveredBy: Friedrich Stromeyer, Karl Samuel Leberecht Hermann
discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: cadmia, calamine, the zinc ore it was found in

summary: A soft, bluish-white metal that absorbs neutrons and is highly toxic, which is why its use is being retired.
uses: Rechargeable batteries, control rods in older reactors, and pigments.
sources: Almost always a by-product of zinc refining.

name: Indium

discovery.nameOrigin: The indigo line in its spectrum

summary: A very soft metal that wets glass, which is what makes it possible to make a transparent electrical contact.
uses: Indium tin oxide, the invisible conductor in a touchscreen and a flat panel display.
sources: A trace in zinc and tin ores, which is the only way it is obtained.

name: Tin

discovery.nameOrigin: Anglo-Saxon: tin; the symbol is from Latin stannum

summary: A soft metal that has been alloyed with copper to make bronze since prehistory, and whose cold crystalline form crumbles.
uses: Solder, tinplate for food cans, and bronze.
sources: Cassiterite, the ore that made the Bronze Age possible.

name: Antimony

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: anti and monos, not alone, because it is never found uncombined

summary: A brittle metalloid that makes other materials harder and refuses to catch fire.
uses: Flame retardants, lead-acid battery plates, and semiconductors.
sources: Stibnite, a striking needle-shaped mineral.

name: Tellurium

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: tellus, earth

summary: A metalloid that is rarer than platinum, and that changes its electrical behaviour when light shines on it.
uses: Thin-film solar panels, and alloying to make steel easier to machine.
sources: Recovered from the anode slimes left behind by copper refining.

name: Iodine

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: iodes, violet-coloured, from the colour of its vapour

summary: A dark solid that sublimes straight to a violet vapour, and an element the human body cannot do without.
uses: Disinfectants, photographic film as silver iodide, and the small dietary supplement that keeps a thyroid working.
sources: Brine and seaweed, and the caliche deposits of Chile.

name: Xenon

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: xenon, stranger, for the unfamiliar gas left in a sample

summary: A heavy inert gas that, despite the name it was given, does form compounds when pushed hard enough.
uses: Car headlamps, ion thrusters for spacecraft, and a general anaesthetic.
sources: The air, at less than one part in ten million, separated by cooling air until it liquefies.

name: Caesium

discovery.discoveredBy: Robert Bunsen, Gustav Kirchhoff, Glenn Theodore Seaborg, Margaret Melhase
discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: caesius, sky blue, from the colour of its spectrum lines

summary: A soft golden metal that melts at room temperature and reacts with water explosively; the second is the standard unit of time.
uses: Atomic clocks, which define the second; photoelectric cells; and drilling fluids.
sources: Pollucite, and as a by-product of lithium refining.

name: Barium

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: barys, heavy, because its minerals are unusually dense

summary: A soft, reactive metal whose insoluble sulphate is swallowed by patients because it blocks X-rays and passes straight through.
uses: A contrast medium for medical imaging, drilling mud, and green colour in fireworks.
sources: Barite, a common mineral that is also the main source of the barium used in oil wells.

name: Lanthanum

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: lanthanein, to lie hidden

summary: The first of the lanthanides, a soft metal that gives the group its name and was hidden in a mixture of rare earths for years.
uses: Camera lenses with low dispersion, hybrid car batteries, and fluid catalytic cracking.
sources: Bastnasite and monazite, the two main rare earth ores.

name: Cerium

discovery.discoveredBy: Martin Heinrich Klaproth, Jöns Jacob Berzelius
discovery.nameOrigin: The asteroid Ceres

summary: The most abundant of the rare earths, and a metal that will strike a spark when scraped.
uses: Polishing powders for glass, catalytic converters, and lighter flints.
sources: Bastnasite and monazite, where it is the commonest rare earth present.

name: Praseodymium

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: prasios and didymos, green twin, from the colour of its salt

summary: A soft silvery metal that tints glass and enamel a clear yellow-green.
uses: Colouring glass and enamel, and very strong permanent magnets when alloyed with neodymium.
sources: Monazite and bastnasite, separated from the other rare earths with some difficulty.

name: Neodymium

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: neos and didymos, new twin

summary: A rare earth metal that gives the strongest permanent magnets in commercial use.
uses: Magnets in headphones, hard drives, wind turbines and electric motors; and a violet colour in glass.
sources: Monazite and bastnasite.

name: Promethium

discovery.discoveredBy: Charles D. Coryell, Lawrence E. Glendenin, Jacob Akiba Marinsky
discovery.nameOrigin: Prometheus, who stole fire from the gods

summary: A radioactive rare earth with no stable isotope, and the only lanthanide that takes a long search to find in nature.
uses: Nuclear batteries, and luminous paint in the past.
sources: Produced in reactors from the fission of uranium; only traces occur in nature.

name: Samarium

discovery.nameOrigin: The mineral samarskite, named after a Russian mine official

summary: A rare earth metal that stays magnetic at high temperatures, which is what makes it useful in a motor.
uses: Samarium-cobalt magnets that work when hot, and neutron absorbers in reactors.
sources: Monazite and bastnasite.

name: Europium

discovery.nameOrigin: Europe

summary: A soft rare earth metal that glows red when it is energized, which is the basis of every bright red phosphor.
uses: Red phosphors in displays and fluorescent lamps, and anti-counterfeiting marks on banknotes.
sources: Bastnasite and monazite.

name: Gadolinium

discovery.nameOrigin: Johan Gadolin, the Finnish chemist who first isolated a rare earth

summary: A rare earth metal that is unusually good at catching neutrons and unusual in that it warms up when it enters a magnetic field.
uses: A contrast agent for MRI scans, neutron shielding, and magnetic refrigeration research.
sources: Monazite and bastnasite.

name: Terbium

discovery.nameOrigin: Ytterby, the Swedish village that named four elements

summary: A soft, silvery rare earth metal whose alloys change shape when magnetized.
uses: Green phosphors in lamps and displays, and magnetostrictive alloys for sonar.
sources: Monazite, bastnasite and xenotime.

name: Dysprosium

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: dysprositos, hard to get at

summary: A rare earth metal that keeps a magnet working at the temperatures inside an electric motor.
uses: High-temperature permanent magnets, and control rods in reactors.
sources: Xenotime and monazite.

name: Holmium

discovery.discoveredBy: Per Teodor Cleve, Marc Delafontaine, Jacques-Louis Soret
discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: Holmia, Stockholm

summary: A rare earth metal with the strongest magnetic moment of any element.
uses: The strongest magnets known when its moment is concentrated; and glass that filters certain wavelengths.
sources: Monazite and gadolinite.

name: Erbium

discovery.nameOrigin: Ytterby, the Swedish village that named four elements

summary: A soft rare earth metal whose ions amplify light, which is what makes a long-distance optical cable possible.
uses: Optical fibre amplifiers, and pink colouring in glass.
sources: Xenotime and euxenite.

name: Thulium

discovery.nameOrigin: Thule, the ancient name for the far north

summary: The rarest of the stable rare earths, soft and silvery, and in demand for one specific job.
uses: A portable X-ray source, and the highest-temperature superconductor behaviour known.
sources: Monazite, in very small quantities.

name: Ytterbium

discovery.nameOrigin: Ytterby, the Swedish village that named four elements

summary: A soft rare earth metal that has become the standard way of measuring time with light.
uses: Optical atomic clocks, the most accurate timekeepers built; and stainless steel.
sources: Monazite, euxenite and xenotime.

name: Lutetium

discovery.discoveredBy: Georges Urbain, Carl Auer von Welsbach
discovery.nameOrigin: Lutetia, the Latin name for Paris

summary: The last and densest of the lanthanides, and the element whose placing in the table is still argued over.
uses: A catalyst for refining petroleum, and detectors in PET scanners.
sources: Monazite, and the only rare earth that is difficult to separate for a second reason: it is rarer than the rest.

name: Hafnium

discovery.nameOrigin: Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen

summary: A corrosion-resistant metal that absorbs neutrons readily, which is exactly the opposite of what zirconium, its constant companion, does.
uses: Control rods in reactors, and superalloys for jet engines.
sources: Zircon, where it always accompanies zirconium and has to be separated from it.

name: Tantalum

discovery.nameOrigin: Tantalus of Greek myth, because the metal refuses to absorb acid

summary: A hard, blue-grey metal that is almost completely immune to attack by acid.
uses: Capacitors small enough for a phone, surgical implants, and chemical plant vessels.
sources: The mineral tantalite, found with niobium.

name: Tungsten

discovery.nameOrigin: Swedish: tung sten, heavy stone; the symbol is from wolframite

summary: The metal with the highest melting point of all, and the one that stays solid when everything else has run.
uses: Cutting tools, drill bits, the filament of an incandescent lamp, and radiation shielding.
sources: Wolframite and scheelite.

name: Rhenium

discovery.discoveredBy: Ida Noddack, Walter Noddack, Otto Berg
discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: Rhenus, the Rhine

summary: One of the rarest elements in the crust, and the one with the highest boiling point of any element known.
uses: Superalloys for the hottest parts of a jet engine, and platinum-rhenium catalysts.
sources: Recovered from the flue dust of molybdenum roasting, which is the only practical source.

name: Osmium

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: osme, smell, from the pungent oxide it forms

summary: The densest naturally occurring element, and dense enough that a litre of it weighs more than twenty kilograms.
uses: Fountain pen nibs and instrument pivots, where hardness matters more than cost; electrical contacts.
sources: Platinum ores, and the residue left after refining them.

name: Iridium

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: iris, rainbow, from the many colours of its salts

summary: The most corrosion-resistant metal known, and the marker in the clay layer that records the impact that ended the dinosaurs.
uses: Spark plugs, crucibles for growing crystals, and the standard kilogram of old.
sources: Platinum ores, and as a trace in meteorites, which is how it was found in that clay.

name: Platinum

discovery.discoveredBy: Julius Caesar Scaliger, Antonio de Ulloa
discovery.nameOrigin: Spanish: platina, little silver, a term of contempt for a metal that would not melt

summary: A dense, unreactive precious metal that is unusually good at making a chemical reaction go faster.
uses: Catalytic converters, laboratory equipment, jewellery, and the electrodes of a fuel cell.
sources: Native metal in river gravels, and in sulphide ores with nickel and copper.

name: Gold

discovery.nameOrigin: Anglo-Saxon: gold; the symbol is from Latin aurum

summary: A dense yellow metal that does not tarnish, can be beaten thinner than a wavelength of light, and has been money for six thousand years.
uses: Jewellery and reserves, electrical contacts, and the reflective coating on a spacecraft.
sources: Native metal in quartz veins and river gravels, and recovered from copper refining.

name: Mercury

discovery.nameOrigin: The planet Mercury, and Latin hydrargyrum, water-silver

summary: The only metal that is liquid at room temperature, dense enough to float iron, and poisonous in a way that took centuries to notice.
uses: Historically thermometers and barometers, and now mostly in compact fluorescent lamps and chemical manufacture.
sources: Cinnabar, from which it is roasted out as a vapour.

name: Thallium

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: thallos, a green shoot, from the bright green line in its spectrum

summary: A soft grey metal once used as a rat poison and now avoided, because it is as toxic to people as to rats.
uses: Historically rat poison and ant bait; now infrared detectors and high-temperature superconductors.
sources: As a trace in lead, zinc and copper ores.

name: Lead

discovery.nameOrigin: Anglo-Saxon: lead; the symbol is from Latin plumbum

summary: A heavy, soft, easily worked metal that is pleasant to use and damages the nervous system, which is why it has been removed from petrol and paint.
uses: Lead-acid batteries, radiation shielding, and the ballast of a keel.
sources: Galena, which is mostly lead sulphide and very easy to smelt.

name: Bismuth

discovery.nameOrigin: German: weisse Masse, white mass

summary: A brittle pinkish-white metal that forms the most spectacular crystals of any element as it cools.
uses: A replacement for lead in plumbing and shot, and stomach medicine; and, as bismuth telluride, thermoelectric cooling.
sources: Native metal, and as a by-product of refining lead, copper and tin.

name: Polonium

discovery.nameOrigin: Poland, the birthplace of Marie Curie

summary: A radioactive metal so intensely radioactive that a sample glows blue and warms itself, discovered in pitchblende.
uses: An alpha source for antistatic devices, and, historically, a heat source for spacecraft.
sources: In uranium ores, at about one part in ten thousand billion; made in reactors.

name: Astatine

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: astatos, unstable

summary: The rarest naturally occurring element, and so radioactive that a visible sample has never existed.
uses: Research, and investigation into targeted cancer therapy.
sources: Fleeting decay products in uranium and thorium ores; less than a gram exists in the whole crust at any moment.

name: Radon

discovery.discoveredBy: Robert Bowie Owens, Friedrich Ernst Dorn, Ernest Rutherford
discovery.nameOrigin: From radium, the element it is produced by

summary: A heavy radioactive gas that seeps out of the ground and concentrates indoors, and the leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.
uses: Historic use in cancer treatment; now a hazard to be ventilated away rather than a tool.
sources: Produced by the decay of radium in soil, rock and building stone.

name: Francium

discovery.nameOrigin: France

summary: The most unstable of the first 101 elements, with a half-life of twenty-two minutes, so no one has ever seen a piece of it.
uses: Research only; its most commonly quoted use is as an example of something that exists only fleetingly.
sources: Decay product in uranium ores, where a few thousand atoms exist at a time.

name: Radium

discovery.nameOrigin: Latin: radius, ray, for the radiation it gives off

summary: A radioactive metal that glows faintly and was once considered a health tonic, before the people who painted watch dials with it began to die.
uses: Historically luminous paint and cancer therapy, both abandoned when the harm became clear.
sources: Pitchblende and other uranium ores at a few parts per million.

name: Actinium

discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: aktis, ray, from its radioactivity

summary: A soft, silvery radioactive metal that glows blue in the dark and gives the actinides their name.
uses: A neutron source, and targeted alpha therapy in research.
sources: Trace amounts in uranium ores; made in reactors for practical use.

name: Thorium

discovery.nameOrigin: Thor, the Norse god of thunder

summary: A weakly radioactive metal that is three times as abundant as uranium and has been proposed as a safer nuclear fuel.
uses: Gas mantles, high-refractive-index glass, and experimental reactor fuel.
sources: Monazite sand, where it is the main radioactive component.

name: Protactinium

discovery.discoveredBy: Kazimierz Fajans, Otto Hahn, Lise Meitner
discovery.nameOrigin: Greek: protos, first, and actinium, because it decays into actinium

summary: A dense, silvery, highly radioactive metal that is rarer than radium and difficult to handle.
uses: Research, and dating sediments and rock by its decay.
sources: Uranium ores, at about one part in ten million.

name: Uranium

discovery.nameOrigin: The planet Uranus, discovered shortly before the element

summary: A dense, weakly radioactive metal whose heaviest natural isotope splits under a neutron, releasing energy in a chain that either powers a city or does something much worse.
uses: Fuel for nuclear reactors, and the source of the plutonium used in weapons; also, because it is dense, armour and counterweights.
sources: Pitchblende and uraninite, at a few parts per million in the crust, and dissolved in sea water.

name: Neptunium

discovery.nameOrigin: The planet Neptune

summary: The first transuranium element to be made, and the first produced in quantity rather than in traces.
uses: A neutron detector, and the precursor from which plutonium is made.
sources: Produced in reactors from uranium; traces occur naturally in uranium ores.

name: Plutonium

discovery.discoveredBy: Joseph W. Kennedy, Arthur Wahl, Glenn Theodore Seaborg, Edwin McMillan
discovery.nameOrigin: The dwarf planet Pluto

summary: A silvery radioactive metal that is warm to the touch from its own decay, and the element whose name most people meet in a context they would rather not.
uses: Reactor fuel and nuclear weapons; and a long-lived isotope that powers deep-space probes.
sources: Manufactured in reactors; only traces occur naturally.

name: Americium

discovery.nameOrigin: The Americas, since it sits below europium

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal that is mildly luminous, which is why it was once found in almost every household.
uses: Ionisation smoke detectors, and industrial thickness gauges.
sources: Produced in reactors from plutonium; not found in nature in meaningful amounts.

name: Curium

discovery.nameOrigin: Marie and Pierre Curie

summary: A hard, silvery radioactive metal that glows purple in the dark and is intensely dangerous to handle.
uses: An alpha source for spectrometers on Mars rovers, and the power source of a pacemaker battery in the past.
sources: Made in reactors; not found in nature.

name: Berkelium

discovery.discoveredBy: Stanley Gerald Thompson, Albert Ghiorso, Glenn Theodore Seaborg
discovery.nameOrigin: Berkeley, California, where it was made

summary: A soft, silvery radioactive metal produced one atom at a time in the first sample ever assembled.
uses: Research, chiefly as a target for making still heavier elements.
sources: Made in reactors; not found in nature.

name: Californium

discovery.discoveredBy: Stanley Gerald Thompson, Kenneth Street Jr., Albert Ghiorso, Glenn Theodore Seaborg
discovery.nameOrigin: The state and University of California

summary: A radioactive metal that throws off neutrons so freely that a small sample is a usable neutron source.
uses: Starting a reactor, finding water and oil underground, and detecting explosives.
sources: Made in reactors; not found in nature.

name: Einsteinium

discovery.nameOrigin: Albert Einstein

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal first identified in the debris of a hydrogen bomb test.
uses: Research only; it is made in quantities of micrograms.
sources: Made in reactors; not found in nature.

name: Fermium

discovery.nameOrigin: Enrico Fermi

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal that has never been made in a quantity anyone could see.
uses: Research only: it is made in quantities nobody can see, so there is nothing to use it for.
sources: Discovered in the fallout of the first hydrogen bomb test; not found in nature.

name: Mendelevium

discovery.nameOrigin: Dmitri Mendeleev, who arranged the table

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal made an atom at a time, and named after the man who first predicted where it would sit.
uses: Research only: atoms are made one at a time by bombarding einsteinium with helium nuclei.
sources: Made by bombarding einsteinium with helium; not found in nature.

name: Nobelium

discovery.nameOrigin: Alfred Nobel

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal whose most stable isotopes last about an hour.
uses: Research only: it is made by firing carbon ions at curium, a few atoms per experiment.
sources: Made by bombarding curium with carbon ions; not found in nature.

name: Lawrencium

discovery.nameOrigin: Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron

summary: The last of the actinides, and the element whose position in group three is the most argued-over question in the table.
uses: Research only: it settles a long argument about which element belongs in group three.
sources: Made by bombarding californium with boron ions; not found in nature.

name: Rutherfordium

discovery.nameOrigin: Ernest Rutherford, who first split an atom

summary: The first of the transactinides, and an element whose chemistry has been studied only a handful of atoms at a time.
uses: Research only: it exists for seconds, and is studied to see whether it behaves like hafnium.
sources: Made by fusing plutonium with neon nuclei; not found in nature.

name: Dubnium

discovery.discoveredBy: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Joint Institute for Nuclear Research
discovery.nameOrigin: Dubna, the Russian town with a heavy-element laboratory

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal whose longest-lived isotope lasts about a day, longer than most of its neighbours.
uses: Research only: its chemistry has been examined a few atoms at a time, in solution.
sources: Made by fusing americium with neon nuclei; not found in nature.

name: Seaborgium

discovery.nameOrigin: Glenn Seaborg, who made ten of the transuranium elements

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal, and the one element named for a person while that person was still alive.
uses: Research only: it is made by fusing lighter nuclei and studied for under a minute.
sources: Made by fusing californium with oxygen nuclei; not found in nature.

name: Bohrium

discovery.nameOrigin: Niels Bohr

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal produced only a few atoms at a time, with a half-life measured in seconds.
uses: Research only: a few atoms at a time, from a machine that runs for weeks to make them.
sources: Made by fusing bismuth with chromium nuclei; not found in nature.

name: Hassium

discovery.discoveredBy: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
discovery.nameOrigin: Hesse, the German state where it was made

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal whose chemistry has been shown to resemble osmium, which was not a given.
uses: Research only: it is used to test whether the heaviest elements still follow the table.
sources: Made by fusing lead with iron nuclei; not found in nature.

name: Meitnerium

discovery.discoveredBy: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
discovery.place: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
discovery.nameOrigin: Lise Meitner, who explained nuclear fission

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal made a few atoms at a time, with no measured chemistry to place it by.
uses: Research only: no use is possible for an element that exists for a few seconds.
sources: Made by fusing bismuth with iron nuclei; not found in nature.

name: Darmstadtium

discovery.discoveredBy: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
discovery.place: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
discovery.nameOrigin: Darmstadt, the German city where it was made

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal whose heaviest known isotopes survive for seconds.
uses: Research only: identified by the trail of alpha particles its decay leaves behind.
sources: Made by fusing lead with nickel nuclei; not found in nature.

name: Roentgenium

discovery.discoveredBy: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
discovery.place: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
discovery.nameOrigin: Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal, and one of the last whose expected behaviour is a prediction rather than a measurement.
uses: Research only: studied to see whether relativity changes how the heaviest metals behave.
sources: Made by fusing bismuth with nickel nuclei; not found in nature.

name: Copernicium

discovery.discoveredBy: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
discovery.nameOrigin: Nicolaus Copernicus

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal that may behave like a gas rather than a metal, which is a strange thing to say about the element under mercury.
uses: Research only: it may be a gas at room temperature, which no other metal is.
sources: Made by fusing lead with zinc nuclei; not found in nature.

name: Nihonium

discovery.nameOrigin: Nihon, a Japanese name for Japan, the country where it was made

summary: The first element discovered in Asia, and one whose every property is an extrapolation from the column above it.
uses: Research only: made a few atoms at a time in a heavy-ion accelerator.
sources: Made by fusing bismuth with zinc nuclei; not found in nature.

name: Flerovium

discovery.nameOrigin: The Flerov Laboratory in Dubna

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal that is expected to be a volatile metal, which would set it apart from every other member of its group.
uses: Research only: its volatility is the property worth measuring, and there is barely enough to measure.
sources: Made by fusing plutonium with calcium nuclei; not found in nature.

name: Moscovium

discovery.nameOrigin: Moscow, and the region around Dubna

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal with a half-life of a fraction of a second and no measured chemistry at all.
uses: Research only: its atoms last a fraction of a second, long enough to identify and no longer.
sources: Made by fusing americium with calcium nuclei; not found in nature.

name: Livermorium

discovery.nameOrigin: The Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory

summary: A synthetic radioactive metal whose atoms survive for milliseconds, so almost nothing about it is more than predicted.
uses: Research only: it is identified by its decay products rather than by anything it does.
sources: Made by fusing curium with calcium nuclei; not found in nature.

name: Tennessine

discovery.nameOrigin: Tennessee, the American state with a heavy-element laboratory

summary: The heaviest halogen, and probably not really a halogen: relativity is expected to pull it towards behaving like a metal.
uses: Research only: its chemistry would settle whether it is a halogen, and there is too little to try.
sources: Made by fusing berkelium with calcium nuclei; not found in nature.

name: Oganesson

discovery.nameOrigin: Yuri Oganessian, who made several of the heaviest elements

summary: The heaviest element yet made, a noble gas that is predicted not to behave like one, and probably a solid rather than a gas.
uses: Research only: a few atoms have ever existed, which leaves nothing to use.
sources: Made by fusing californium with calcium nuclei; only a few atoms have ever existed.
